newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten coy about post-Hong Kong ambitions.
newsitem.headline: Patten coy about post-Hong Kong ambitions.

text.p: Chris Patten, the 28th and last governor of the British colony of Hong Kong, was once tipped as a possible future prime minister.
But Patten was effectively sidelined by the spectacular rise of another politician of his generation, John Major, who replaced Margaret Thatcher as Conservative Party premier in 1990.
When Patten, credited with helping engineer Major's unexpected general election victory in 1992, lost his parliamentary seat, Major quickly offered the party chairman the key Hong Kong post.

Within weeks of his arrival in Britain's last Asian outpost, Patten found himself on a path to confrontation with China which furiously rejected democratic reforms the British planned to introduce in response to populist demands.

Patten nevertheless pressed on despite an almost total breakdown in Sino-British relations and saw his modest reform package bear fruit when Hong Kong went to the polls in September 1994 to return its first ever elected legislature, free of appointed members.

China, which still objects to the reforms, has said it would dissolve the legislature when it resumes sovereignty of the British colony next year, and the dispute remains the main source of friction between London and Beijing.
Patten has been coy about his ambitions for his future when his governorship ends at midnight on June 30, 1997.

Commentators and fellow politicians have argued that taking the governorship of the colony make it difficult if not impossible for Patten to return to elected politics but that has not dampened speculation that he may still harbour such ambitions.
Patten had always been something of an outsider in the British establishment and is credited with having risen on his own abilities and skills.

A Roman Catholic intellectual, he penetrated the highest levels of the Conservative ruling class. He was a backer of former prime minister Edward Heath and stood firm on his vision of interventionist Conservatism that would be egalitarian and benignly paternalistic.
He holds strongly to his Catholicism. He has said that his religious upbringing was "in the great hellfire tradition" and that he has a "fairly well-developed sense of guilt".

Elected in the 1979 election which swept Thatcher to power, Patten joined her cabinet in July 1989 as environment secretary, having served in junior ministerial posts including Northern Ireland and the Foreign Office.
Although his background was on the left of the Conservative Party his intellect and wit found him a home in the Thatcher cabinet and an easy transition to Major's.

Chris Patten was born in May 1944 and educated at a Catholic school in west London. He then studied at Balliol College, Oxford, where he read modern history. He also studied in the United States on a Coolidge Travelling Scholarship.
He and his wife Lavender have three daughters.
